pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Hemileia vastatrix Berk. and Broome (Basidiomycota, Pucciniales) was described in 1869 in eastern Africa and Ceylon as the agent of coffee leaf rust

type_of_disease.quote: Hemileia vastatrix is a hemicyclic fungus producing urediniospores, teliospores and basidiospores

affected_parts.quote: The disease symptoms and signs include large orange spore masses on the lower leaf surface, leading to premature leaf fall

summary.value: Chlorotic spots appear first on leaves, followed by suprastomatal, bouquet-shaped, orange-coloured uredinia (large orange spore masses) on the lower leaf surface, leading to premature leaf fall.
summary.quote: Chlorotic spots are the first macroscopic symptoms, preceding the differentiation of suprastomatal, bouquet	stomatal, bouquet-shaped, orange-coloured uredinia.

diagnostic_features.value: Suprastomatal, bouquet-shaped, orange-coloured uredinia (orange pustules) protruding through the stomata on the lower leaf surface approximately 3 weeks after infection; chlorotic spots as the first macroscopic symptom; premature leaf fall/severe defoliation.
diagnostic_features.quote: Approximately 3 weeks after infection, urediniosporic sori protrude through the stomata in a bouquet shape. These appear as orange-coloured pustules, the typical sign of this disease

value: Hemileia coffeicola (produces sori scattered throughout the leaf and presents urediniospores with fewer but larger spines)
look_alikes.quote: Hemileia vastatrix can be distinguished from H. coffeicola , as the latter produces sori scattered throughout the leaf and presents urediniospores with fewer but larger spines.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: the etiological agents of phoma spot are fungi Phoma tarda (RB Stewart) H. Verm. and Phoma costarricensis Echandi, 1957 (Pleosporales: Didymellaceae)

type_of_disease.quote: The phoma stain, Phoma spp., is a fungal disease that occurs in several countries around the world where coffee is grown in areas of higher altitudes.

affected_parts.quote: the fungus attacks leaves, flowers, fruits and branches of the coffee plant, producing very characteristic lesions

summary.value: On leaves, the disease produces circular dark spots of varying sizes (up to 2 cm in diameter); on affected branches, dark depressed lesions appear that can involve the entire diameter (dry shoots); it can also cause necrosis of flowers and fruits in floral rosettes.
summary.quote: On the leaves of the second and subsequent pairs of leaves, the disease produces circular spots of dark color and varying sizes, which can reach 2 cm in diameter (Fig. 2). In the affected branches, a symptom also called dry shoots (Fig. 3), dark depressed lesions are seen, which can involve the entire diameter.

diagnostic_features.value: Infection begins at the apical part in terminal shoots and tender leaves; when lesions reach leaf edges, leaves curve and may present cracks; circular dark spots up to 2 cm on older leaves; dark depressed lesions on branches that can involve the entire diameter (dry shoots); necrosis of flowers and fruits in floral rosettes.
diagnostic_features.quote: the infection begins at the apical part, in the terminal shoot, in the tender leaves, which still have no physical barriers of resistance, reaching the young tissues. When the lesions reach the edges of the leaves, they curve, may present cracks

look_alikes.quote: the symptom can easily be confused with boron deficiency (Fig. 1)

conflicts.note: The journal article uses the generic 'Phoma spp.' while the Cultivar article specifies the two known etiological agents as Phoma tarda and Phoma costarricensis. The more specific identification from Cultivar is preferred as the canonical value.

The Springer article mentions leaf lesions, drying of branches, and rotting of flowers and fruits but lists only Foliar and Stem as primary parts. The Cultivar article explicitly lists leaves, flowers, fruits, and branches.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Mycosphaerella coffeicola is the name of the sexual form of the fungus; the disease is also known by the asexual form, Cercospora coffeicola.

type_of_disease.quote: Mycosphaerella coffeicola is the name of the sexual form of the fungus

affected_parts.quote: Small brown spots occur on the leaves... On the berries, the infections are smaller than on leaves... In nurseries, it can cause leaf fall of seedlings and, in severe cases, stem dieback.

summary.value: Small brown spots on leaves with light brown or grey centres, surrounded by a wide dark brown ring and a yellow margin; on berries, smaller irregular brown spots appear mainly on the sun-exposed side.
summary.quote: Small brown spots occur on the leaves, more obvious on the upper surface... they have light brown or sometimes light grey centres, surrounded by a wide, dark brown ring, and a yellow margin

diagnostic_features.value: Circular brown spots mostly 5-10 mm (up to 15 mm) with bright grey or light brown centres and yellow haloes; spore masses visible in the grey centres of the leaf spots and on blackened ripe berries.
diagnostic_features.quote: Circular brown spots, mostly 5-10 mm, with bright grey centres and yellow haloes, typical of brown-eye leaf spot, Cercospora coffeicola. Spores of the fungus form in the grey centres

conflicts.note: Mycosphaerella coffeicola is the accepted sexual (teleomorph) form; Cercospora coffeicola is the asexual (anamorph) form. The source notes both names are in use. No taxonomy validation data was provided to confirm the currently accepted name under modern nomenclature.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Leucoptera coffeella or Coffee Leaf Miner, is an insect pest not yet found on the Hawaiian islands.

affected_parts.quote: the larvae that feed on the palisade parenchyma of the coffee leaves

summary.value: Larvae feed inside the leaf mesophyll creating mines; pale yellow trails form underneath the coffee leaf epidermis that develop into irregular brown spots on the upper leaf surface; mines cause necrosis and reduce photosynthetic leaf surface, leading to defoliation.
summary.quote: When feeding on the mesophyll of the coffee tree leaves, the insect creates mines that justify the common name of the pest—coffee leaf miner ( Figure 6 a). The mines cause necrosis ( Figure 6 b) and reduce the photosynthetic leaf surface ( Figure 6 c,d), leading to a lower photosynthetic rate of the plants and consequent depletion of the plant and productivity diminish

diagnostic_features.value: Pale yellow mining trails underneath the leaf epidermis developing into irregular brown spots on the upper leaf surface, with the epidermis separating when the affected leaf is bent; light green mines on leaves that darken due to residues left behind by the larva; cocooned pupae typically found on leaves on the lower third of the plant.
diagnostic_features.quote: coffee leaf miner larvae leave pale yellow trails underneath the coffee leaf epidermis. The mining trails then turn into irregular brown spots on upper leaf surface. Physically bending the affected leaf will cause the epidermis to separate. Cocooned pupae are typically found on leaves on the lower third of the plant.
